title: Bergson
content_html:
Bergson

Henri Bergson (1859 – 1941) was a French philosopher whose work reshaped 20th-century thinking about time, consciousness, memory, and creativity. His writing stands at the intersection of metaphysics, psychology, and evolutionary biology, using vivid metaphors to challenge mechanistic conceptions of life and mind.

Year Title Core Idea Relation to Memory
1889 Essai sur les données immédiates de la conscience (Time and Free Will) Distinguishes lived time (durée) from physical/mechanical time; consciousness is continuous flow, not divisible units. Establishes subjective temporality — the inner rhythm in which memory is embedded.
1896 Matière et mémoire (Matter and Memory) Bridges mind and body: perception as selection for action; memory as pure past coexisting with present. Foundational for non-local, layered models of memory (influence on Merleau-Ponty, Deleuze, cognitive phenomenology).
1907 L’Évolution créatrice (Creative Evolution) Life as élan vital — a creative thrust that invents forms through duration; evolution is creative, not mechanistic. Extends memory into biological time, treating life itself as a form of memory.
1911 L’Énergie spirituelle (Mind-Energy) Essays on consciousness, dreams, telepathy, and the relation between mind and brain. Connects memory to psychical energy; anticipates later discussions on brain plasticity and distributed cognition.
1932 Les Deux Sources de la morale et de la religion (The Two Sources of Morality and Religion) Differentiates closed (social-instinctive) and open (creative-mystical) morality; intuition expands social memory. Explores collective memory and ethical creativity — aligns with your Mnemonic Ecology theme.
1934 La Pensée et le mouvant (The Creative Mind) Essays clarifying intuition and analysis, defending metaphysics as direct apprehension of change. Articulates intuition as cognitive memory — knowing through continuity of becoming.

For Bergson, memory is the continuity of becoming itself — the bridge between consciousness and life, past and future, potential and act. His work positions memory not as storage but as duration that endures, making him one of the most crucial metaphysical precursors for your project’s unification of biology, consciousness, and creative evolution.

The qualitative, continuous flow of time is a lived experience, irreducible to spatial measurement. Science spatializes time (seconds, minutes), but lived consciousness endures as overlapping states. Memory is not retrieval of discrete moments but immersion in duration’s continuity, mind and matter are not dual substances but two directions of one process.

  • Perception = selection of what matters for action.
  • Memory = the whole of the past that subsists virtually.
  • Influence: Anticipated theories of embodied cognition, predictive processing, and non-representational mind.

Evolution is creative invention — not predetermined mechanism, the living being is a temporal synthesis; life retains and transforms its past in order to create. Intellect divides and measures (useful for matter), but intuition grasps movement and becoming directly. Intuition therfore reconnects intellect to duration — a kind of higher memory.

Closed morality preserves social memory; open morality extends compassion universally. Memory is the ethical link that unites rather than separates. For Bergson, memory is the continuity of becoming itself — the bridge between consciousness and life, past and future, potential and act. His work positions memory not as storage but as duration that endures, making him one of the most crucial metaphysical precursors for your project’s unification of biology, consciousness, and creative evolution.

Bergson’s durée maps to the idea of continuity that precedes segmentation. Event boundaries in memory research mirror intellect’s spatialization of time. “What cognitive science calls ‘event boundaries’ are the intellect’s way of slicing the continuous flow that Bergson called durée.” Bergson’s pure memory is virtual, coexisting with the present — precisely what constructive models simulate. “The past is preserved by itself, automatically… it endures.”

The élan vital embodies the same triadic process:

  • Select: life differentiates pathways;
  • Change: adapts through variation;
  • Reconstruct: integrates memory into new form.

Evolution is memory at the scale of species — reconstruction as survival. Bergson also viewed dreams as creative recombinations of memory fragments — anticipating consolidation theories. Is dreaming byproduct or essential? Intuition is the sympathy by which one is transported into the interior of an object to coincide with what is unique in it.

Domain Thinkers / Movements Influenced
Phenomenology & Existentialism Husserl, Merleau-Ponty, Sartre — emphasis on lived experience and temporal flow.
Process & Evolutionary Thought Whitehead, Teilhard de Chardin — life as creative process.
Continental Philosophy Deleuze’s Bergsonism reframed duration as multiplicity and memory as virtual.
Cognitive Science & AI Embodied cognition, enactive mind, temporal coding models echo Bergson’s dynamic perception.
Art & Literature Proust’s In Search of Lost Time is an artistic elaboration of Bergsonian memory; modernist art used durée to explore movement and consciousness.
